metadata.title: On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit
metadata.author: Odo of Tournai (Odo of Cambrai)
known_issues: Several biblical citations are printed only by chapter, without verse numbers; they have been rendered exactly in spoken form and explained in notes where relevant.
The source text refers to a diagram explaining four opposites, but the diagram itself is not present in the supplied Latin; it has not been reconstructed.
Odo’s reference to “the malicious Jews” reflects medieval polemical language and is contextually limited in the translation to the hostile opponents in the Gospel scene.
The printed citation “II Cor. XIV” is spoken as printed, but the quoted material corresponds to Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verses fourteen and sixteen.
The quotation attributed to Ezekiel chapter thirty-three is a traditional paraphrase rather than an exact Vulgate wording.
The printed reading “sul sermonis” appears corrupt for “sui sermonis”; the translation follows the evident sense and notes the issue.
The Latin clause “quae totum quidquid est, vera dilectio est” is awkward in the printed text; the translation follows the probable theological sense rather than a wooden rendering.

The printed Gospel references use a nonstandard scheme: Matthew, chapter twelve; Mark, chapter thirty-four; and Luke, chapter forty-seven. The quotations correspond to Matthew chapter twelve, verses thirty-one through thirty-two; Mark chapter three, verses twenty-eight through thirty; and Luke chapter twelve, verse ten.
The phrase “in Joanne” has been identified as the First Letter of John because of the wording “sin leading to death,” but Odo gives no explicit citation.

corrections.original: So if God forgives pride in an unrepentant person, God would be forgiving something against himself. He would be joining to himself the very thing that cuts every good thing off from him. He would be uniting himself to that which every good thing resists.
corrections.corrected: So if God forgives the unrepentant, he forgives pride directed against himself; he joins to himself the very thing that cuts every good off from him, and unites himself to that which every good resists.
corrections.latin: Si ergo Deus impoenitenti dimittit superbiam sibi dimittit, et id sibi adjungit quod a se bonum omne disjungit, idque sibi consociat cui bonum omne repugnat.
corrections.reason: operator reading: 'superbiam sibi dimittit' = forgives pride [aimed] at himself; the earlier rendering rearranged the clauses and blurred the object

corrections.original: then it would be false. For blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven without repentance.
corrections.corrected: then it would be false. For it to be true, the qualification “through repentance” must not be understood in it; for blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven without repentance.
corrections.latin: Quae ut vera sit, non est intelligendus poenitentiae modus; nam sine poenitentia non potest remitti Spiritus blasphemia.
corrections.reason: omitted clause restored (severity 3 omission found by the reviewer, confirmed against the Latin)

corrections.original: Rather, it loves all things as created things. Indeed, if divine love did not love every being, no single thing could exist as it does.
corrections.corrected: Rather, it loves all things — that love which, in the whole of what it is, is true love. For unless it loved every being, not even one thing could exist as it is.
corrections.latin: sed diligit omnia, quae totum quidquid est, vera dilectio est, nisi enim essentiam omnem diligeret, unum quoque sicut est esse non potest.
corrections.reason: 'quae totum quidquid est, vera dilectio est' qualifies love itself (in the whole of what it is, it is true love); 'as created things' was an invention

corrections.original: For what love truly loves, it gladly forgives when it has been offended.
corrections.corrected: For the love that truly loves gladly forgives an offence.
corrections.latin: Nam quae vere diligit, libenter offensam dimittit.
corrections.reason: 'quae' is the subject (she who truly loves), 'offensam' the object; the earlier rendering inverted them

corrections.original: And the injury that most wickedly rejects pardon for sins most deeply grieves the Holy Spirit.
corrections.corrected: And whatever repels the pardon of sins with greater wickedness offends the Holy Spirit with greater injury.
corrections.latin: et injuria majori sanctum molestat Spiritum quod majori nequitia veniam repellit peccatorum.
corrections.reason: 'injuria majori' is ablative and 'quod … repellit' the subject; the earlier rendering made the injury the agent

corrections.corrected: Therefore, seeing by divine knowledge their impenitence to the end, Christ declared that they were to be condemned forever, and he instructed later generations to beware so great an evil.
corrections.latin: Inde divinitus cernens eorum usque ad finem impoenitentiam, et eos in aeternum damnandos dicebat, et posteros ut tantum malum caveant instruebat.
corrections.reason: 'dicebat' is a main verb ('he declared that they were to be condemned forever'), not something Christ merely saw; 'Christ spoke as he did' was a paraphrase

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Treatise on the Unforgivable Sin
chunks.latin: DE BLASPHEMIA IN SPIRITUM SANCTUM
chunks.english: On Blasphemy against the Holy Spirit

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why Odo Takes Up the Question
chunks.latin: Prologus.
chunks.english: Prologue.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
[Col. 1111D]

De blasphemia sancti Spiritus se conscripsisse libellum dicit in Enchiridio beatus Augustinus. Sed hic liber in meas manus non incidit, nec aliquem scio me vidisse qui legerit. Unde conquerebatur mecum vir venerabilis Amandus, Acquicinotensis monachus, quod tantae quaestionis solutio non inveniretur anxius. Erat enim mihi tunc Acquicinotus dulce refugium exsilii mei, quia potestate regia pellebar a sede Cameracensi, quod virgam et annulum, quae [Col. 1112D] consecratus ab Ecclesia acceperam, dono imperatoris iterum accipere non acquiescebam. Cumque frater praedictus, mecum saepe loquens de spiritualibus, praedictae quaestionis solutionem a me devotus exigeret, mittebam eum ad expositiones orthodoxorum Patrum. Sed dicebat eos non tractare secundum modos dubitationis suae nec per eorum expositionem auferri sibi posse dubitationem. Itaque melius mihi visum est onus suscipere, (licet sit ruendum) quam penitus negando, superbiam putet, vel contemptum, [Col. 1113A] et malo ut videat me non posse sudando fatiscentem quam se repulsae pudeat, me postponente laborem. Animavit etiam multum libellus De originali peccato, quem noviter conscripseram, in quo aestuanti mihi occurrerunt multa quae nesciebam.
chunks.english:
In his Enchiridion, blessed Augustine says that he wrote a little book on blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. But that book has never come into my hands, and I do not know that I have ever met anyone who had read it.

For this reason, a venerable man named Amandus, a monk of Anchin, used to speak with me anxiously and complain that no solution could be found to so great a question. At that time Anchin was a sweet refuge for me in my exile. I had been driven by royal power from the see of Cambrai, because I would not agree to receive again, as a gift from the emperor, the staff and ring that I had already received from the Church when I was consecrated.

This brother often spoke with me about spiritual matters, and he earnestly kept asking me for a solution to the question just mentioned. I referred him to the explanations of the orthodox Fathers. But he said that they did not address the precise forms his doubt took, and that their explanations could not remove his uncertainty.

So it seemed better to me to take up the burden, even if I should stumble under it, than by refusing outright to make him think I was acting from pride or contempt. I would rather have him see me sweating and exhausted because I cannot manage the task, than have him feel ashamed of being rejected while I avoid the work. I was also greatly encouraged by the little book On Original Sin, which I had recently written; while I was struggling with that subject, many things came to me that I had not known before.
chunks.notes: “Acquicinotus” refers to Anchin Abbey. “Virgam et annulum,” the staff and ring, refers to the investiture controversy over whether secular rulers could confer episcopal symbols.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Gospel Passages That Raise the Problem
chunks.latin: Quoto canone, quotis capitulis invenitur in Evangelio blasphemia Spiritus.
chunks.english: In Which Canon and Which Chapters Blasphemy against the Spirit Is Found in the Gospel

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Et primum proponenda sunt ipsius Evangelii verba quae faciunt quaestionem, deinde difficultas quaestionis prius est ostendenda quam accingamur ad solutionem. Continentur autem in secundo canone, capitulo Matthaei, cap. XII, et Marci, XXXIV, Lucae vero, XLVII. Matthaeus sic ait: Omne peccatum et blasphemia remittetur hominibus, Spiritus autem blasphemia non remittetur. Et quicunque dixerit verbum contra [Col. 1113B] Filium hominis, remittetur ei: Qui autem dixerit contra Spiritum sanctum, non remittetur ei, neque in hoc saeculo, neque in futuro. Marcus sic: Amen dico vobis quia omnia dimittentur filiis hominum peccata, et blasphemiae quibus blasphemaverint. Qui autem blasphemaverit in Spiritum sanctum, non habet remissionem in aeternum, sed reus erit aeterni delicti. Quia dicebant: Spiritum immundum habet. Lucas autem sic: Omnis qui dicit verbum in Filium hominis remittetur illi. Ei autem qui in Spiritum sanctum blasphemaverit non remittetur.
chunks.english:
First, we must set out the very words of the Gospel that create the question. Then we must show why the question is difficult, before we prepare ourselves to solve it.

These passages are found in the second canon, at section twelve of the Gospel of Matthew, section thirty-four of the Gospel of Mark, and section forty-seven of the Gospel of Luke.

Matthew says: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven human beings, but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.”

Mark says: “Amen, I tell you, all sins will be forgiven the children of men, and all the blasphemies with which they blaspheme. But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever, but will be guilty of an eternal offense.” “Because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’”

Luke says: “Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven. But the one who blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.”
chunks.notes: The printed references are spoken as printed. Mark has no chapter thirty-four, and Luke’s chapter forty-seven is not a modern biblical chapter number; these appear to be older canon or section references. The quotations correspond to Matthew chapter twelve, verses thirty-one through thirty-two; Mark chapter three, verses twenty-eight through thirty; and Luke chapter twelve, verse ten.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Some Sins Can Be Forgiven, One Cannot
chunks.latin: Quod quaedam peccata dimitti possint, quaedam non.
chunks.english: That Some Sins Can Be Forgiven, and Some Cannot

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Ecce tria haec capitula secundi canonis, dicunt omne peccatum posse dimitti praeter unum; unum solum nullo modo consequi posse indulgentiam, omne [Col. 1113C] aliud aliquo modo impetrare veniae misericordiam; unum solum omnino insolubile, omne aliud absolvi posse. Super unum solum puteus urget os suum, ut aeterna claudatur oblivione; super omne aliud patet os putei, ut quoquo modo possit exire. Sed primum videamus quomodo remissibilia peccata dimittat Deus.
chunks.english:
These three Gospel passages in the second canon say that every sin can be forgiven except one. One sin alone can in no way obtain pardon; every other sin can, in some way, receive the mercy of forgiveness. One sin alone is completely unable to be loosed; every other sin can be absolved.

Over that one sin, the pit presses its mouth shut, so that it is closed up in eternal oblivion. Over every other sin, the mouth of the pit stands open, so that somehow it may escape.

But first, let us consider how God forgives sins that can be forgiven.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why God Cannot Forgive the Unrepentant
chunks.latin: Quod impoenitenti non potest peccatum dimitti.
chunks.english: That Sin Cannot Be Forgiven to the Unrepentant

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Aut poenitenti dimittit Deus, aut impoenitenti. Porro impoenitenti nequit dimittere peccatum Deus; nec enim potest injustus esse Deus. Peccat homo in hominem, peccat et in Deum. Impoenitens est in hominem, impoenitens est et in Deum. Impoenitenti debet homo dimittere, nec debet Deus, quia peccator dimittere debet peccatori, Deus autem non debet [Col. 1113D] impoenitenti. Peccator dimittit etiam impoenitenti, quia timet desuper ne sibi non dimittatur etiam poenitenti; non dimittit impoenitenti Deus, quia non timet ne sibi non dimittatur. Peccatori impoenitenti debet homo dimittere, quia et ipse est peccator; Deus non debet, quia non est peccator. Amplius, omnis impoenitentia est superbia, et omnis superbia principaliter est Deo contraria. Si ergo Deus impoenitenti dimittit superbiam sibi dimittit, et id sibi adjungit quod a se bonum omne disjungit, idque sibi consociat cui bonum omne repugnat. Sed impossibile est ut summo bono summum malum confoederetur ullo modo, et ulli malo astipuletur summum bonum, nedum ei quod principaliter habet contrarium. [Col. 1114A] Nam quae participatio luci ad tenebras? (II Cor. XIV.) Quid templo Dei et idolis?
chunks.english:
God forgives either a repentant person or an unrepentant one. But God cannot forgive sin in an unrepentant person, because God cannot be unjust.

A human being sins against another human being, and also sins against God. A person can remain unrepentant toward another human being, and also unrepentant toward God. A human being ought to forgive even an unrepentant person; God ought not to do so. Why? Because a sinner ought to forgive another sinner, but God does not owe forgiveness to the unrepentant.

A sinner forgives even the unrepentant because he fears judgment from above, fearing that he himself may not be forgiven even when he repents. God does not forgive the unrepentant, because God has no fear that forgiveness will be withheld from him. A human being ought to forgive an unrepentant sinner because he too is a sinner. God does not owe that forgiveness, because God is not a sinner.

Furthermore, all impenitence is pride, and all pride is directly opposed to God. So if God forgives the unrepentant, he forgives pride directed against himself; he joins to himself the very thing that cuts every good off from him, and unites himself to that which every good resists.

But it is impossible for the highest good to be allied in any way with the highest evil. The supreme good cannot give support to any evil at all, much less to the evil that is directly opposed to it. As Paul says in his second letter to the Corinthians, chapter fourteen: “What fellowship has light with darkness?” And again: “What agreement has the temple of God with idols?”
chunks.notes: The printed citation is “II Cor. XIV,” rendered in spoken form as chapter fourteen. The quoted phrases correspond to Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, verses fourteen and sixteen.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Goods God Gives but Does Not Perform
chunks.latin: Quod quaedam bona Deus habeat quae ipse facere non potest.
chunks.english: That God Possesses Some Goods Which He Himself Cannot Do

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Si ergo impoenitenti dimittere potest homo, et dimittere non potest Deus, bonum ergo facere potest homo quod facere non potest Deus. Sed unde habet homo bonum nisi ab eo qui est summum bonum? Habet homo magnum bonum, impoenitenti dimittere, magnum bonum, et quod conveniat perfectis tantum. Sed unde hoc habet, si Deus facere non potest ipsum? Certe non habet homo a se tantum bonum, sed a Deo, a quo est omne bonum. Habet enim Deus et hoc bonum, etsi non facit ipsum. In se habet, et a se dat homini quod habet. Habet Deus ut jubeat, accipit homo ut [Col. 1114B] faciat. Non habet in se Deus pro se, habet in se pro homine; non habet in se sibi, habet in se nobis; habet in se, et facimus nos; habet in se, et pertinet ad nos. Sunt ergo bona quae, quamvis nequeat facere Deus, habet ipsa tamen Deus; habet ipsa, quia aliter non faceremus, nisi ab ipso haberemus. Sunt ergo bona congrua Creatoris majestati, sunt bona congrua creaturae servituti. Et haec tamen et illa ab eo sunt a quo et in quo sunt omnia bona.
chunks.english:
If, then, a human being can forgive the unrepentant, while God cannot forgive the unrepentant, it follows that a human being can do a good thing that God cannot do.

But where does a human being get any good, except from the one who is the highest good? A human being has a great good: the ability to forgive an unrepentant person. It is a great good, and one suited only to the perfect. But where does a person get this good, if God himself cannot do it?

Certainly, a human being does not possess so great a good from himself, but from God, from whom every good comes. God possesses even this good, although he does not perform it. God has it in himself, and from himself he gives to human beings what he has. God has it in order to command it; the human being receives it in order to do it.

God does not have it in himself for his own sake, but for the sake of humanity. He does not have it in himself as something for himself, but as something for us. He has it in himself, and we perform it. He has it in himself, and it belongs to us.

Therefore there are good things that God possesses, even though God cannot perform them. He possesses them because we would not do them unless we had them from him. So there are goods fitting for the majesty of the Creator, and there are goods fitting for the service of the creature. Yet both kinds of good come from the one from whom and in whom all good things exist.
chunks.notes: Odo is making a technical distinction: God can be the source of a good action that is proper to creatures, even when that action would be unfitting or impossible for God to perform as God.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.latin: Quod etiam impoenitenti possit dimitti peccatum, si poeniteat.
chunks.english: That Even Impenitence Can Be Forgiven If One Repents

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Etsi nullum peccatum, ut ostensum est, impoenitenti, dimittitur omne peccatum poenitenti. Et forsitan ipsa impoenitentia, quia irremissibilis est, Spiritus est blasphemia. Sed quid? si ipsius impoenitentiae [Col. 1114C] peccatorem poeniteat, et quam diu pertinaciter tenuit tandem dimittat, nunquid veniam meretur, et haec poenitentis impoenitentia dimittitur? Diu impoenitens fuit, et modo poenitet, et longam cordis duritiam nunc emollivit, videmus lacrymas, audimus gemitus, et compunctionem cordis Deus videt intus; si huic clauditur misericordiae janua, cui aperitur? Absit ut hunc Deus repellat, ut hunc misericordissimus amoveat, cum scriptum sit: Quacunque hora ingemuerit peccator, recipiam eum! (Ezech. XXXIII.) Absit ut ulla culpa poenitentis apud summum medicum sit insanabilis! Si ergo impoenitentia, quae videtur irremissibilis, per poenitentiam ipsa remittitur, quae est culpa quae omnino non remittitur, quae blasphemia [Col. 1114D] Spiritus vocetur?
chunks.english:
Although, as we have shown, no sin is forgiven in an unrepentant person, every sin is forgiven in a repentant person.

Perhaps, then, impenitence itself is blasphemy against the Spirit, since impenitence is unforgivable. But what if a sinner repents of that very impenitence? What if he finally lets go of the stubbornness he held for so long? Does he not deserve pardon? Is not the impenitence of a repentant person forgiven?

He was unrepentant for a long time, but now he repents. He has now softened the hardness of heart that lasted so long. We see his tears; we hear his groans; and God sees inwardly the compunction of his heart. If the door of mercy is closed to this person, to whom is it opened?

Far be it from God to reject such a person. Far be it from the most merciful one to push him away, since Scripture says in Ezekiel, chapter thirty-three: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, I will receive him.” Far be it that any guilt in a repentant person should be incurable before the supreme physician.

So if impenitence, which seems unforgivable, is itself forgiven through repentance, then what is the guilt that is not forgiven at all? What sin is called blasphemy against the Spirit?
chunks.notes: The Ezekiel quotation is rendered as printed. It is a traditional paraphrase associated with Ezekiel chapter thirty-three rather than an exact biblical quotation.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.latin: Inquisitio quod peccatum sit blasphemia.
chunks.english: Inquiry: Which Sin Is Blasphemy against the Spirit?

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Ecce hinc Evangelium blasphemiam Spiritus omnino irremissibile clamat, hinc Ecclesia firmissima veritatis columna, contra omne peccatum poenitentiam praedicat. Hinc Evangelium triplici capitulo quoddam peccatum omnino non posse dissolvi confirmat, hinc Ecclesia per poenitentiam de omni peccato certam promittit veniam. Evangelio nefas est contradicere, et Ecclesiam quis audeat falsificare? Quoddam Evangelium negat, omne Ecclesia affirmat. Contradictoriae sunt, nec possunt simul esse verae, si intellectus idem servetur ubique. Diverso igitur modo intelligendae sunt, ut simul verae sint. Inveniatur igitur modus, cujus identitate verum sibi dividuant et falsum, et cujus diversitate sint simul verae. Et universalis affirmatio Ecclesiae, quae peccatum omne posse dicit remitti, vera est, si intelligatur poenitentiae modus. Quid, si intelligatur similiter in singulari negatione Evangelii, quae dicit Spiritus blasphemiam non posse remitti per poenitentiam falsa est? Quae ut vera sit, non est intelligendus poenitentiae modus; nam sine poenitentia non potest remitti Spiritus blasphemia. Ut vero simul sit verum cum Ecclesia Evangelium, intelligamus altrinsecus diversum poenitentiae modum, ut, cum affirmatione Ecclesia ponit intellectum poenitentiae, auferat Evangelium a sua negatione, et simul erit verum, et quod blasphemia Spiritus sine poenitentia non remittitur, et quod omne peccatum per poenitentiam deleatur; et eas unus modus, et dividere sibi verum et falsum faciet idem, et simul esse veras faciet diversus. Talique modo non differt Evangelium ab Ecclesia, cum dicit blasphemiam Spiritus non posse remitti, subintelligendo sine poenitentia, cum hoc idem de omni peccato dicat Ecclesia. Sed mirum est cur Evangelium ab omni peccato excipit blasphemiam, cum, sicut omne peccatum, remitti possit per poenitentiam, sed credo, quia ideo est mirum, quia nondum mihi est apertum ostium. Aperi, Christe, pulsanti, revela mysteria sanctissimi verbi. Dicis omne peccatum posse remitti, praeter Spiritus blasphemiam, nec ullum potest dimitti, nisi per poenitentiam, nunquid et blasphemiam non sequitur poenitentia? Forsan hoc dicet aliquis, quia tam grande peccatum est Spiritus blasphemia ut ejus nulla possit sequi poenitentia. Et licet aliquis blasphemus videatur pectus tundere, audiatur et suspirare, dicetur forsitan quia non fit hoc ex corde, sed sic ad infinitum mittimur, ut incerta judicemus et scientiam inscrutabilis abyssi cordis humani praesumptuose jactemus, et occultam profunditatem, quam scire solius est Dei nos penetrare clamemus. Cum blasphemi videamus tunsiones pectoris, et lacrymas, et audiamus profundos gemitus et longa suspiria, quis audeat dolosum dicere, nec ex corde poenitere? Non credo summam sapientiam hoc scribi voluisse in Evangelio quod capere non possit homo, nec id hominem docere quod homo non possit scire. Et ideo nondum comprehendisse me arbitror Spiritus blasphemiam quae non dimittitur, ne fingere cogar cordis impoenitentiam quae nescitur.
chunks.english:
So here is the problem. On one side, the Gospel cries out that blasphemy against the Spirit is absolutely unforgivable. On the other side, the Church, that firmest pillar of truth, preaches repentance in response to every sin. On one side, the Gospel confirms in three passages that a certain sin cannot be loosed at all. On the other side, the Church promises sure pardon for every sin through repentance.

It would be wicked to contradict the Gospel; and who would dare accuse the Church of falsehood? The Gospel denies forgiveness for one particular sin; the Church affirms forgiveness for every sin. These statements are contradictory, and they cannot both be true if they are understood in exactly the same sense. So they must be understood in different senses, so that both can be true.

We must find the distinction: in one sense, the statements separate truth from falsehood; in another sense, they allow both statements to stand as true. The Church’s universal affirmation—when it says that every sin can be forgiven—is true if it is understood as speaking about forgiveness through repentance. But if the Gospel’s particular denial—when it says that blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven—were understood in the same way, as meaning that it cannot be forgiven through repentance, then it would be false. For it to be true, the qualification “through repentance” must not be understood in it; for blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven without repentance.

So, if the Gospel is to be true together with the Church, we must understand a different relation to repentance in each statement. When the Church affirms forgiveness, it includes repentance: every sin is forgiven through repentance. When the Gospel denies forgiveness, it excludes repentance: blasphemy against the Spirit is not forgiven without repentance. In that way, both are true: blasphemy against the Spirit is not forgiven without repentance, and every sin is wiped away through repentance. The same idea of repentance separates true from false; the different application of that idea lets both statements be true.

Understood in this way, the Gospel does not differ from the Church. When it says that blasphemy against the Spirit cannot be forgiven, we understand, “without repentance.” And the Church says the same thing about every sin.

But then another puzzle remains. Why does the Gospel single out blasphemy from all other sins, when, like every other sin, it can be forgiven through repentance? I think this seems puzzling because the door has not yet been opened to me. Open it, Christ, to the one who knocks. Reveal the mysteries of your most holy word.

You say that every sin can be forgiven except blasphemy against the Spirit, and yet no sin can be forgiven except through repentance. Does repentance not follow blasphemy too? Perhaps someone will say, “Blasphemy against the Spirit is such a great sin that no repentance can ever follow it.” And even if some blasphemer seems to beat his breast, and is heard sighing, perhaps it will be said that he is not doing this from the heart.

But then we are sent off into endless uncertainty. We start judging what cannot be known, and we presumptuously claim knowledge of the unsearchable abyss of the human heart. We shout that we can penetrate a hidden depth which only God can know. When we see blasphemers beating their breasts and shedding tears, and when we hear deep groans and long sighs, who would dare say that the repentance is deceitful and not from the heart?

I do not believe that supreme Wisdom wanted something written in the Gospel which a human being cannot grasp, or wanted to teach a human being something that a human being cannot know. And therefore I think I have not yet understood what the unforgiven blasphemy against the Spirit is; otherwise I would be forced to invent an unknowable impenitence of the heart.
chunks.notes: Odo frames the contradiction as logical: the Church’s teaching is universal, the Gospel’s exception is particular. His initial solution is that the Gospel denies forgiveness only where repentance is absent.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Sin Leading to Death and Blasphemy against the Spirit
chunks.latin: Quod peccatum ad mortem sit blasphemia Spiritus.
chunks.english: That the Sin unto Death Is Blasphemy against the Spirit

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Sed requiratur Joannis evangelistae prima Epistola, quae canonicarum Epistolarum est una, in qua dicitur aliquid Evangelio simile. Videtur enim per Epistolam concordasse tribus evangelistis in hoc verbo, de quo nihil posuerat in Evangelio suo, quasi in Epistola suppleat quod minus in Evangelio dixerat, ut haec sententia quam quaerimus ex hoc sciatur firmior quo confirmata est ab evangelistis quatuor. Audivimus tres evangelistas quid dixerint unde fit quaestio. Audiamus Joannem quartum quid dixerit, unde fiat solutio. Tres implicant nos suorum verborum obscuritate, quartus nos explicat sul sermonis evidenti manifestatione. Dicit enim: Est peccatum ad mortem, pro quo dico ut non oret quis (I Joan. V). Cur pro eo prohibetur orandum, nisi quia nullo modo est remittendum? Pro eo certe orandum non est quod omnino dimitti non potest. Et hoc evangelista vocat peccatum usque ad mortem, ut qui in peccato claudit extremum diem, culpam habeat irremissibilem, pro qua nullum Deus admittit orantem Haec est blasphemia Spiritus, quae non remittitur, cum quis usque ad finem peccato tenetur, ut illum excipiat aeterna poena, quem cum voluntate peccandi deserit haec vita. Talis peccator in hoc saeculo non absolvitur, quia in voluntate permansit peccandi, neque in futuro, quia cum voluntate peccandi transiit. Et juste punitur semper qui vellet peccare semper, si viveret in hoc saeculo semper, ut voluntatem peccandi sempiternam poena comitetur sempiterna, ut non deficiat in eo poenae justae necessitas in quo non deficit peccandi voluntas.
chunks.english:
But we should consult the first letter of John the Evangelist, one of the canonical letters, where something similar to the Gospel is said. In that letter, John seems to agree with the three evangelists on this saying, even though he had not included it in his own Gospel. It is as though, in the letter, he supplies what he had left unsaid in the Gospel, so that the teaching we are investigating may be known as more firmly established because it is confirmed by all four evangelists.

We have heard what the three evangelists said, and from their words the question arises. Now let us hear what John, the fourth evangelist, says, and from his words the solution will arise. The three entangle us by the obscurity of their words; the fourth disentangles us by the clear revelation of his own speech.

For he says, in John’s first letter, chapter five: “There is a sin leading to death; I do not say that anyone should pray for that.” Why is prayer for that sin forbidden, unless because it is in no way to be forgiven? Certainly one should not pray for something that cannot be forgiven at all.

And the Evangelist calls this a sin “unto death”: the person who closes his final day while still in sin has an unforgivable guilt, and God admits no one to pray for it. This is the blasphemy against the Spirit which is not forgiven: a person is held by sin right up to the end, so that eternal punishment receives the one whom this life leaves behind still willing to sin.

Such a sinner is not absolved in this age, because he remained in the will to sin. Nor is he absolved in the age to come, because he passed out of this life with the will to sin. And it is just that he be punished forever, because he would have wanted to sin forever if he had lived forever in this age. An everlasting punishment follows an everlasting will to sin, so that the necessity of just punishment does not fail in the person whose will to sin does not fail.
chunks.notes: The printed citation gives only “I Joan. V,” rendered here as “John’s first letter, chapter five.” The quoted text corresponds to First John chapter five, verse sixteen. The printed text has “sul sermonis,” evidently for “sui sermonis”; the translation follows the evident sense, “his own speech.”

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: How One Final Sin Includes Every Unforgiven Sin
chunks.latin: Quomodo peccatum ad mortem unum solum peccatum sit, sicut Spiritus blasphemia.
chunks.english: How the Sin unto Death Is One Single Sin, Just as Blasphemy against the Spirit Is

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Hic oritur quaestio valde difficilis, quod evangelistae tres unum solum peccatum in Evangelio dicunt irremissibile, scilicet blasphemiam Spiritus, separantes eam ab omnibus aliis, evangelista vero Joannes in Epistola nullum separatim dicit irremissibile, sed peccatum usque mortem qualecunque. Quomodo conveniunt Epistola Joannis et Evangelium, si quod Evangelium de omni negat praeter unum nominatum, hoc Joannes de quolibet affirmat, non de uno separatim? Dicit Evangelium: Sola blasphemia Spiritus est irremissibilis; dicit Joannes: Quodlibet peccatum usque ad mortem nullam meretur orationem.

Evangelium singulariter nominat blasphemiam Spiritus et determinate, Epistola nil singulariter nominat, sed peccatum usque ad mortem dicit indeterminate. Peccatum ad mortem indeterminate dictum intelligimus quodlibet unum indefinite, blasphemia spiritus intelligitur peccatum non quodlibet, sed unum definite.

Et Epistola Joannis hoc modo dissentire videtur ab Evangelio, cum Epistola dicat quodlibet peccatum ad mortem, pro quo non sit orandum; et Evangelium dicat solam blasphemiam Spiritus irremissibile peccatum.
chunks.english:
Here a very difficult question arises. The three evangelists say in the Gospel that only one sin is unforgivable, namely blasphemy against the Spirit, and they separate it from all other sins. But John the Evangelist, in his letter, does not name any one sin separately as unforgivable. Instead, he speaks of any sin at all, if it continues up to death.

How, then, do John’s letter and the Gospel agree? The Gospel denies this of every sin except one named sin; John affirms it of any sin whatever, and not of one sin separately. The Gospel says, “Only blasphemy against the Spirit is unforgivable.” John says, “Any sin that continues unto death deserves no prayer.”

The Gospel names blasphemy against the Spirit in a singular and definite way. The letter names nothing singularly, but speaks indefinitely of a sin unto death. When “sin unto death” is spoken of indefinitely, we understand it as any one sin, without specifying which. But “blasphemy against the Spirit” is understood not as just any sin, but as one definite sin.

In this way, John’s letter seems to disagree with the Gospel: the letter says that no one should pray for any sin that leads to death, while the Gospel says that blasphemy against the Spirit alone is the unforgivable sin.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Sed hanc quaestionem sicut implicat inconsiderata rerum confusio, sic explicat eam rerum diligenter considerata discretio. Adjacet enim cuilibet peccato poenitentia, vel pertinacia; poenitentia bonum, peccatum ipsum malum; pertinacia peccati ad tempus, pejus; pertinacia ad mortem pessimum, et ultimum malum. Itaque malorum aliud prius, aliud posterius, aliud postremum. Prius, ut fornicatio, furtum, rapina, odium, invidia et alia infinita; posterius, ut impoenitentia ad tempus; postremum, ut impoenitentia ad ultimum.

Et priora praecedunt quasi capitalia, de quibus, habeatur poenitentia vel impoenitentia. Nisi enim primum peccatum fiat, non est cujus poeniteat aliquem, vel cujus impoenitens maneat. Ab omni malo ad primum bonum prius diriguntur, id est, poenitentiam, quam sequitur remissio. A primo malo caditur in posterius, inde ad postremum, quod est ad finem impoenitentia, quam sequitur irremissio. In quae duo, id est posterius et postremum, peccator cum venerit, contemnit (Prov. XVIII).
chunks.english:
But the problem is tangled only when we confuse things without thinking carefully. It is untangled when we distinguish them with care.

Beside every sin there stands either repentance or obstinacy. Repentance is good. The sin itself is evil. Obstinacy in sin for a time is worse. Obstinacy all the way to death is worst of all; it is the final evil.

So among evils, one comes first, another later, and another last. The first evils are things like fornication, theft, robbery, hatred, envy, and countless others. The later evil is impenitence for a time. The last evil is impenitence to the very end.

The first evils come before the others, like primary sins, and with respect to them a person may have either repentance or impenitence. For unless the first sin is committed, there is nothing for which someone may repent, or in which someone may remain impenitent.

From any evil, a person is first directed toward the first good, that is, repentance; forgiveness follows it. But from the first evil, a person may fall into the later evil, and from there into the last evil, which is impenitence to the end; unforgiveness follows that. When the sinner comes into those two evils—the later and the last—he becomes contemptuous, as Scripture says in the Book of Proverbs, chapter eighteen.
chunks.notes: The printed citation gives only “Prov. XVIII,” rendered in spoken form as “the Book of Proverbs, chapter eighteen.” The wording alludes to Proverbs chapter eighteen, verse three, but no verse number is printed.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Hic considerantur quatuor contraria, duo bona, duobus malis opposita. Quorum ratio ut evidentius appareat, sic ea quadrata formula disponat ut linea superior e regione duo contineat, et linea inferior e regione duo similiter habeat. Et sic apparet in utrisque lineis eorum prima fronte contrarietas. Et sic in utrisque lateribus inveniuntur, ut ad se invicem sequantur. Hinc duo bona per misericordiam, inferius virtutis, superius palmae; inde duo mala per justitiam, inferius culpae, superius poenae; angulariter vero sic utrinque repugnant ut simul esse nequeant, duo immutabilitate justitiae, duo certitudine misericordiae, ut subjecta monstrat descriptio.

Hoc ergo modo considerata discretione rerum, cum in Evangelio dicitur omne dimitti peccatum, intelliguntur ipsa peccata quae sunt prius, et impoenitentia ad tempus, quae est posterius. Spiritus vero blasphemia, quae remitti non potest, est impoenitentia ad finem, pro qua orari non debet. Et cum in Evangelio multa sint et innumerabilia peccata, quae possunt dimitti, una est Spiritus blasphemia, quae non potest dimitti, cui est idem in Epistola Joannis peccatum ad mortem, id est impoenitentia ad finem, pro quo solo non debet orari. Et ita est unum solum peccatum irremissibile et in tribus evangelistis et in Joanne, appellatum in Evangelio Spiritus blasphemia, in Epistola vero peccatum ad mortem, id est impoenitentia ad finem.
chunks.english:
Here we should consider four opposites: two goods set against two evils. To make the relation clearer, imagine them arranged as a square. The upper line contains two things facing each other; the lower line likewise contains two things facing each other. In both lines, the direct opposition is clear. Along the two sides, the terms are related as things that follow one another.

On one side are the two goods that come through mercy: below, the good of virtue; above, the good of reward. On the other side are the two evils that come through justice: below, the evil of guilt; above, the evil of punishment. Diagonally, the terms oppose each other in such a way that they cannot coexist: two by the unchangeable character of justice, and two by the certainty of mercy, as the diagram below is meant to show.

So, when these distinctions are carefully considered, the Gospel’s statement that every sin is forgiven refers to the sins that come first, and also to impenitence for a time, which comes later. But blasphemy against the Spirit, which cannot be forgiven, is impenitence to the end, for which one should not pray.

Thus, although the Gospel speaks of many, indeed countless, sins that can be forgiven, there is one blasphemy against the Spirit that cannot be forgiven. This is the same as what John’s letter calls “the sin leading to death,” that is, impenitence to the end, for which alone one should not pray. Therefore, both in the three evangelists and in John, there is only one unforgivable sin: in the Gospel it is called blasphemy against the Spirit; in the letter it is called the sin leading to death, meaning impenitence to the end.
chunks.notes: The source refers to a “diagram below,” but the supplied text contains no recoverable diagram, only a blank space between column markers. The translation preserves Odo’s verbal explanation without reconstructing the diagram.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Why the Unforgivable Sin Is Assigned to the Spirit
chunks.latin: Cur irremissibilis blasphemia magis pertinet ad Spiritum quam ad Patrem vel Filium.
chunks.english: Why the Unforgivable Blasphemy Belongs to the Spirit Rather than to the Father or the Son

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Sed cum in Joanne signanter et proprie peccatum ad mortem vocetur, quaeritur in Evangelio cur blasphemia non Patris, vel Filii, sed Spiritus tantum dicatur. Ad quod respondetur quia, cum majestas summae Trinitatis tota sit charitas et in summa Trinitate singula quaeque persona certissime sit charitas, tamen Spiritus sanctus specialiter et proprie est, charitas, quia Patris et Verbi est vera communio, et dulcis utriusque ad invicem et ad omnia dilectio. Et cum ipsa charitas nequeat admittere suum [Col. 1118B] contrarium, non potest odisse quidquam quod sit creatum, sed diligit omnia, quae totum quidquid est, vera dilectio est, nisi enim essentiam omnem diligeret, unum quoque sicut est esse non potest. Quaedam autem essentiae culpam admiserunt, sed et ipsas vera charitas diligit quae peccaverunt, parata ad indulgentiam, si agant poenitentiam. Nam quae vere diligit, libenter offensam dimittit.
chunks.english: But since John marks this out and calls it, in a special sense, “a sin leading to death,” the question arises in the Gospel: why is it called blasphemy not against the Father, or against the Son, but only against the Spirit? The answer is this. The majesty of the supreme Trinity is wholly love, and each person in the supreme Trinity is most certainly love. Yet the Holy Spirit is love in a special and proper sense, because he is the true communion of the Father and the Word, and the sweet love by which they love one another and all things. And because love itself cannot admit its own opposite, it cannot hate anything that has been created. Rather, it loves all things — that love which, in the whole of what it is, is true love. For unless it loved every being, not even one thing could exist as it is. Some beings, however, have fallen into guilt. But true love loves even those who have sinned, and is ready to pardon them if they repent. For the love that truly loves gladly forgives an offence.
chunks.notes: “In Joanne” is best understood as referring to the First Letter of John and its phrase “sin leading to death,” though Odo gives no chapter or verse. The column marker is editorial and is not spoken. The clause “quae totum quidquid est, vera dilectio est” is syntactically difficult; the translation gives the evident sense that divine love, precisely as love, loves every created being in its being, not its guilt.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Est enim verae charitatis officium, optata remissio peccatorum. Et, sicut in summa Trinitate charitas proprie refertur ad Spiritum, ita proprie ascribitur Spiritui remissio peccatorum, utpote charitatis officium; quamvis in tota Trinitate commune sit peccata dimittere.
chunks.english: For the forgiveness of sins is the work that true love desires. And just as, within the supreme Trinity, love is properly related to the Spirit, so too the forgiveness of sins is properly ascribed to the Spirit, because forgiveness is the work of love. Even so, the power to forgive sins belongs in common to the whole Trinity.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 1118C] Si ergo Spiritus sanctus proprie peccata dimittit, id certe contra Spiritum sanctum se magis erigit quod remissionem peccatorum magis excludit, et injuria majori sanctum molestat Spiritum quod majori nequitia veniam repellit peccatorum. Et ideo recte vocatur blasphemia Spiritus illud peccatum quod charitatis dulce refutat officium, nec accipere curat munus veniae, quod charitas omnibus optat impertire. Et hoc est peccatum ad mortem, id est impoenitentia ad finem, extremum malum, irremissibile solum, cum remitti possit aliud omne peccatum. Et hoc est contra sanctum Spiritum dicere, scilicet divina opera vituperando et in pravam partem ducendo, invidiose et superbe usque in finem impoenitentem persistere, sicut et malitiosi Judaei [Col. 1118D] tunc faciebant, qui divinas ejus virtutes immundo spiritui ascribebant. Inde divinitus cernens eorum usque ad finem impoenitentiam, et eos in aeternum damnandos dicebat, et posteros ut tantum malum caveant instruebat. Invenimus ex his Evangelii capitulis aliter loqui Patres orthodoxos; quae qui vult scire requirat apud illos.
chunks.english: So if the Holy Spirit is the person to whom the forgiveness of sins is properly attributed, then whatever most decisively shuts out the forgiveness of sins rises up most directly against the Holy Spirit. And whatever repels the pardon of sins with greater wickedness offends the Holy Spirit with greater injury. That is why this sin is rightly called blasphemy against the Spirit: it refuses the sweet work of love and does not care to receive the gift of pardon, which love desires to give to everyone. This is the sin leading to death: final impenitence, the ultimate evil, the only sin that cannot be forgiven, while every other sin can be forgiven. And this is what it means to speak against the Holy Spirit: by slandering divine works and twisting them into an evil interpretation, a person persists, enviously and proudly, without repentance all the way to the end. That is what the malicious Jews were doing at that time, when they attributed Christ’s divine powers to an unclean spirit. Therefore, seeing by divine knowledge their impenitence to the end, Christ declared that they were to be condemned forever, and he instructed later generations to beware so great an evil. We do find the orthodox Fathers speaking in other ways about these Gospel passages. Anyone who wants to know their interpretations should consult their writings.
chunks.notes: The column markers are editorial and are not spoken. “Judaei” is translated as “Jews” because that is the printed text; in context Odo is referring specifically to the hostile Jewish opponents in the Gospel narrative, not to all Jewish people. “Ejus virtutes” is rendered “Christ’s divine powers” to make the referent explicit for audio listeners.
